claim: Many photosynthetic organisms employ a CO2 concentrating mechanism (CCM) to increase the rate of CO2 fixation via the Calvin cycle.
source: Many photosynthetic organisms employ a CO2 concentrating mechanism (CCM) to increase the rate of CO2 fixation via the Calvin cycle.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about photosynthetic organisms.

claim: CCMs catalyze approximately 50% of global photosynthesis.
source: CCMs catalyze ≈50% of global photosynthesis, yet it remains unclear which genes and proteins are required to produce this complex adaptation.
evidence: This statement cites a specific quantitative estimate about the contribution of CCMs to global photosynthesis, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Expression of 20 CCM genes enabled E. coli to grow by fixing CO2 from ambient air into biomass.
source: Expression of 20 CCM genes enabled E. coli to grow by fixing CO2 from ambient air into biomass, with growth in ambient air depending on the components of the CCM.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Growth in ambient air depends on the components of the CCM.
source: Expression of 20 CCM genes enabled E. coli to grow by fixing CO2 from ambient air into biomass, with growth in ambient air depending on the components of the CCM.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that mutations to CCM components ablate growth in ambient air.

claim: Bacterial CCMs are genetically compact and readily transplanted.
source: Bacterial CCMs are therefore genetically compact and readily transplanted, rationalizing their presence in diverse bacteria.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the successful reconstitution of the CCM with only 20 genes.

claim: Nearly all carbon in the biosphere enters by CO2 fixation in the Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle.
source: Nearly all carbon in the biosphere enters by CO2 fixation in the Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle (Bassham, 2003; Bassham et al., 1954; Benson, 2002; Field et al., 1998; Raven, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to established scientific literature.

claim: Rubisco is the CO2 fixing enzyme in the Calvin cycle.
source: Ribulose Bisphosphate Carboxylase/Oxygenase - commonly known as rubisco - is the CO2 fixing enzyme in this cycle (Kawashima and Wildman, 1971; Weissbach et al., 1956; Wildman, 2002) and likely the most abundant enzyme on Earth (Bar-On and Milo, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature.

claim: Rubisco is likely the most abundant enzyme on Earth.
source: Ribulose Bisphosphate Carboxylase/Oxygenase - commonly known as rubisco - is the CO2 fixing enzyme in this cycle (Kawashima and Wildman, 1971; Weissbach et al., 1956; Wildman, 2002) and likely the most abundant enzyme on Earth (Bar-On and Milo, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bar-On and Milo, 2019.

claim: Photosynthetic rubiscos have carboxylation turnover numbers (kcat) ranging from 1 to 10 s−1.
source: Photosynthetic rubiscos are modest enzymes, with carboxylation turnover numbers (kcat) ranging from 1 to 10 s−1 (Badger et al., 1998; Flamholz et al., 2019; Iñiguez et al., 2020; Jordan and Ogren, 1983; Savir et al., 2010; Tcherkez et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to scientific literature providing kinetic measurements.

claim: All known rubiscos catalyze a competing oxygenation of ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate.
source: Moreover, all known rubiscos catalyze a competing oxygenation of the five-carbon organic substrate, ribulose 1, 5-bisphosphate (Bathellier et al., 2018; Bowes and Ogren, 1972; Cleland et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature.

claim: Rubisco oxygenation fails to generate any new organic carbon.
source: Rubisco oxygenation represents a 'waste' of cellular resources on two fronts: it fails to generate any new organic carbon and also produces a molecule (2-phosphoglycolate) that is not part of the Calvin cycle and therefore must be recycled through a salvage pathway to keep the cycle going (Busch, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and draws from established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Rubisco oxygenation produces 2-phosphoglycolate that must be recycled through a salvage pathway.
source: Rubisco oxygenation represents a 'waste' of cellular resources on two fronts: it fails to generate any new organic carbon and also produces a molecule (2-phosphoglycolate) that is not part of the Calvin cycle and therefore must be recycled through a salvage pathway to keep the cycle going (Busch, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and draws from established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Rubisco arose more than 2.5 billion years ago.
source: Rubisco arose >2.5 billion years ago, when Earth's atmosphere contained little O2 and abundant CO2 (Fischer et al., 2016; Shih et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature on the evolutionary history of rubisco.

claim: When rubisco arose, Earth's atmosphere contained little O2 and abundant CO2.
source: Rubisco arose >2.5 billion years ago, when Earth's atmosphere contained little O2 and abundant CO2 (Fischer et al., 2016; Shih et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature on ancient atmospheric composition.

claim: Present-day atmosphere contains approximately 0.04% CO2.
source: Present-day atmosphere, however, poses a problem for plants and other autotrophs: their primary carbon source, CO2, is relatively scarce (≈0.04%) while a potent competing substrate, O2, is abundant (≈21%).
evidence: This is established knowledge about atmospheric composition.

claim: Present-day atmosphere contains approximately 21% O2.
source: Present-day atmosphere, however, poses a problem for plants and other autotrophs: their primary carbon source, CO2, is relatively scarce (≈0.04%) while a potent competing substrate, O2, is abundant (≈21%).
evidence: This is established knowledge about atmospheric composition.

claim: CO2 concentrating mechanisms arose multiple times over the last 2 billion years.
source: CO2 concentrating mechanisms (CCMs) arose multiple times over the last 2 billion years (Flamholz and Shih, 2020; Raven et al., 2017) and overcame rubisco's limitations by concentrating CO2 near the enzyme (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature on CCM evolution.

claim: CCMs overcome rubisco's limitations by concentrating CO2 near the enzyme.
source: CO2 concentrating mechanisms (CCMs) arose multiple times over the last 2 billion years (Flamholz and Shih, 2020; Raven et al., 2017) and overcame rubisco's limitations by concentrating CO2 near the enzyme (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: High CO2 increases the rate of carboxylation and competitively inhibits oxygenation.
source: As such, high CO2 is expected to increase the rate of carboxylation and competitively inhibit oxygenation (Bowes and Ogren, 1972) thereby improving overall carbon assimilation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: At least four varieties of CCMs are found in plants, algae, and bacteria.
source: Today, at least four varieties of CCMs are found in plants, algae, and bacteria (Flamholz and Shih, 2020; Raven et al., 2017), organisms with CCMs are collectively responsible for ≈50% of global net photosynthesis (Raven et al., 2017), and some of the most productive human crops (e.g. maize and sugarcane) rely on CCMs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature.

claim: Organisms with CCMs are collectively responsible for approximately 50% of global net photosynthesis.
source: Today, at least four varieties of CCMs are found in plants, algae, and bacteria (Flamholz and Shih, 2020; Raven et al., 2017), organisms with CCMs are collectively responsible for ≈50% of global net photosynthesis (Raven et al., 2017), and some of the most productive human crops (e.g. maize and sugarcane) rely on CCMs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Raven et al., 2017.

claim: Some of the most productive human crops (e.g. maize and sugarcane) rely on CCMs.
source: Today, at least four varieties of CCMs are found in plants, algae, and bacteria (Flamholz and Shih, 2020; Raven et al., 2017), organisms with CCMs are collectively responsible for ≈50% of global net photosynthesis (Raven et al., 2017), and some of the most productive human crops (e.g. maize and sugarcane) rely on CCMs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about crop physiology.

claim: The bacterial CCM consists of at least two essential components: energy-coupled inorganic carbon uptake and carboxysome structures.
source: The bacterial CCM consists of at least two essential components - energy-coupled inorganic carbon uptake and carboxysome structures that encapsulate rubisco with a carbonic anhydrase (CA) enzyme (Desmarais et al., 2019; Kaplan et al., 1980; Price and Badger, 1989a, Price and Badger, 1989b; Rae et al., 2013; Shively et al., 1973).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Carboxysomes encapsulate rubisco with a carbonic anhydrase enzyme.
source: The bacterial CCM consists of at least two essential components - energy-coupled inorganic carbon uptake and carboxysome structures that encapsulate rubisco with a carbonic anhydrase (CA) enzyme (Desmarais et al., 2019; Kaplan et al., 1980; Price and Badger, 1989a, Price and Badger, 1989b; Rae et al., 2013; Shively et al., 1973).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Inorganic carbon transport generates a large cytosolic HCO3- pool.
source: Transport generates a large cytosolic HCO3- pool, which is rapidly converted to high carboxysomal CO2 concentration by the carboxysomal CA (Mangan et al., 2016; McGrath and Long, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Carboxysomal carbonic anhydrase converts cytosolic HCO3- to high carboxysomal CO2 concentration.
source: Transport generates a large cytosolic HCO3- pool, which is rapidly converted to high carboxysomal CO2 concentration by the carboxysomal CA (Mangan et al., 2016; McGrath and Long, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: H. neapolitanus CCM genes are mostly contained in a 20 gene cluster.
source: H. neapolitanus CCM genes are mostly contained in a 20 gene cluster (Desmarais et al., 2019) expressing rubisco and its associated chaperones (green), carboxysome structural proteins (purple), and an inorganic carbon transporter (orange).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The 20 gene cluster expresses rubisco and its associated chaperones, carboxysome structural proteins, and an inorganic carbon transporter.
source: H. neapolitanus CCM genes are mostly contained in a 20 gene cluster (Desmarais et al., 2019) expressing rubisco and its associated chaperones (green), carboxysome structural proteins (purple), and an inorganic carbon transporter (orange).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: CCMs are particularly common among autotrophic bacteria.
source: CCMs are particularly common among autotrophic bacteria: all Cyanobacteria and many Proteobacteria have CCM genes (Kerfeld and Melnicki, 2016; Rae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature.

claim: All Cyanobacteria have CCM genes.
source: CCMs are particularly common among autotrophic bacteria: all Cyanobacteria and many Proteobacteria have CCM genes (Kerfeld and Melnicki, 2016; Rae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature.

claim: Many Proteobacteria have CCM genes.
source: CCMs are particularly common among autotrophic bacteria: all Cyanobacteria and many Proteobacteria have CCM genes (Kerfeld and Melnicki, 2016; Rae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature.

claim: Carboxysomes are 200+ MDa protein organelles.
source: Bacterial CCMs rely on two crucial features: (i) energy-coupled inorganic carbon uptake at the cell membrane and (ii) a 200+ MDa protein organelle called the carboxysome that encapsulates rubisco with a carbonic anhydrase enzyme (Desmarais et al., 2019; Kaplan et al., 1980; Price and Badger, 1989a, Price and Badger, 1989b; Rae et al., 2013; Shively et al., 1973).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to scientific literature.

claim: In the prevailing model of the carboxysome CCM, inorganic carbon uptake produces a high, above-equilibrium cytosolic HCO3- concentration of approximately 30 mM.
source: In the prevailing model of the carboxysome CCM (Fridlyand et al., 1996; Mangan et al., 2016; McGrath and Long, 2014), inorganic carbon uptake produces a high, above-equilibrium cytosolic HCO3- concentration (≈30 mM) that diffuses into the carboxysome, where carbonic anhydrase activity produces a high carboxysomal CO2 concentration that promotes efficient carboxylation by rubisco (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to modeling studies and illustrated in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Cytosolic HCO3- diffuses into the carboxysome where carbonic anhydrase produces high carboxysomal CO2 concentration.
source: In the prevailing model of the carboxysome CCM (Fridlyand et al., 1996; Mangan et al., 2016; McGrath and Long, 2014), inorganic carbon uptake produces a high, above-equilibrium cytosolic HCO3- concentration (≈30 mM) that diffuses into the carboxysome, where carbonic anhydrase activity produces a high carboxysomal CO2 concentration that promotes efficient carboxylation by rubisco (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to modeling studies and illustrated in Figure 1A-B.

claim: There is great interest in transplanting CCMs into crops.
source: As CCMs accelerate CO2 fixation by rubisco, there is great interest in transplanting them into crops (Ermakova et al., 2020; McGrath and Long, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature on crop engineering.

claim: Carboxysome-based CCMs natively function in single cells.
source: Carboxysome-based CCMs are especially attractive because they natively function in single cells and appear to rely on a tractable number of genes (Lin et al., 2014; Long et al., 2018; Occhialini et al., 2016; Orr et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations and draws from established knowledge about bacterial physiology.

claim: Carboxysome-based CCMs appear to rely on a tractable number of genes.
source: Carboxysome-based CCMs are especially attractive because they natively function in single cells and appear to rely on a tractable number of genes (Lin et al., 2014; Long et al., 2018; Occhialini et al., 2016; Orr et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature.

claim: Modeling suggests that introducing bacterial CCM components could improve plant photosynthesis.
source: Modeling suggests that introducing bacterial CCM components could improve plant photosynthesis (McGrath and Long, 2014), especially if aspects of plant physiology can be modulated via genetic engineering (Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to modeling studies.

claim: Expressing bacterial rubiscos and carboxysome components has uniformly resulted in transgenic plants displaying impaired growth.
source: However, expressing bacterial rubiscos and carboxysome components has, so far, uniformly resulted in transgenic plants displaying impaired growth (Lin et al., 2014; Long et al., 2018; Occhialini et al., 2016; Orr et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies in plants.

claim: Current understanding of the carboxysome CCM rests mostly on loss-of-function genetic experiments in native hosts.
source: More generally, as our understanding of the genes and proteins participating in the carboxysome CCM rests mostly on loss-of-function genetic experiments in native hosts (Baker et al., 1998; Cai et al., 2009; Cannon et al., 2001; Desmarais et al., 2019; Marcus et al., 1986; Ogawa et al., 1987; Price and Badger, 1989a), it is possible that some genetic, biochemical, and physiological aspects of CCM function remain unappreciated.
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies in native hosts.

claim: A genome-wide screen in H. neapolitanus demonstrated that a 20-gene cluster encodes all activities required for the CCM.
source: Using a genome-wide screen in the CO2-fixing proteobacterium Halothiobacillus neapolitanus, we recently demonstrated that a 20-gene cluster encodes all activities required for the CCM, at least in principle (Desmarais et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The 20-gene cluster includes rubisco large and small subunits, the carboxysomal carbonic anhydrase, seven structural proteins of the α-carboxysome, an energy-coupled inorganic carbon transporter, three rubisco chaperones, and four genes of uncertain function.
source: These genes are detailed in Supplementary file 1 and include rubisco large and small subunits, the carboxysomal carbonic anhydrase, seven structural proteins of the ɑ-carboxysome (Bonacci et al., 2012), an energy-coupled inorganic carbon transporter (Desmarais et al., 2019; USF MCB4404L et al., 2017; Scott et al., 2019), three rubisco chaperones (Aigner et al., 2017; Feiz et al., 2014; Mueller-Cajar, 2017; Wheatley et al., 2014), and four genes of uncertain function (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: E. coli does not natively rely on rubisco.
source: As E. coli is a heterotroph, consuming organic carbon molecules to produce energy and biomass, it does not natively rely on rubisco.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli metabolism.

claim: To grow on glycerol as the sole carbon source, E. coli must synthesize ribose 5-phosphate (Ri5P) for nucleic acids.
source: To grow on glycerol as the sole carbon source, E. coli must synthesize ribose 5-phosphate (Ri5P) for nucleic acids.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli metabolism.

claim: Synthesis of Ri5P via the pentose phosphate pathway forces co-production of ribulose 5-phosphate (Ru5P).
source: Synthesis of Ri5P via the pentose phosphate pathway forces co-production of ribulose 5-phosphate (Ru5P).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the pentose phosphate pathway.

claim: Deletion of ribose 5-phosphate isomerase (rpiAB genes) makes Ru5P a metabolic 'dead-end'.
source: Deletion of ribose 5-phosphate isomerase (rpiAB genes, denoted Δrpi), however, makes Ru5P a metabolic 'dead-end' (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on metabolic pathway knowledge and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Expression of phosphoribulokinase (prk) and rubisco enables a 'detour' pathway converting Ru5P and CO2 into two units of 3-phosphoglycerate (3PG).
source: Expression of phosphoribulokinase (prk) and rubisco enables a 'detour' pathway converting Ru5P and CO2 into two units of the central metabolite 3-phosphoglycerate (3PG), enabling Ru5P metabolism and growth (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Cytosolic carbonic anhydrase activity is incompatible with the bacterial CCM.
source: Additionally, cytosolic carbonic anhydrase activity is incompatible with the bacterial CCM (Price and Badger, 1989b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to scientific literature.

claim: CCMB1 lacks rpiAB and all endogenous carbonic anhydrases.
source: We therefore constructed a strain, named CCMB1 for 'CCM Background 1', lacking rpiAB and all endogenous carbonic anhydrases (Materials and methods, Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental strain construction.

claim: CCMB1 required rubisco and prk for growth on glycerol minimal media in 10% CO2.
source: As predicted, CCMB1 required rubisco and prk for growth on glycerol minimal media in 10% CO2 (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: CCMB1:p1A failed to grow on glycerol media in ambient air.
source: CCMB1:p1A failed to grow on glycerol media in ambient air, however, presumably due to insufficient carboxylation at low CO2 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CCMB1:p1A displays the 'high-CO2 requiring' phenotype that is the hallmark of CCM mutants.
source: As such, CCMB1:p1A displays the 'high-CO2 requiring' phenotype that is the hallmark of CCM mutants (Baker et al., 1998; Marcus et al., 1986; Price and Badger, 1989a).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: Four additional bacterial rubiscos enabled CCMB1 to grow reproducibly in high CO2 but not in ambient air.
source: Four additional bacterial rubiscos were tested and displayed the same pattern, enabling CCMB1 to grow reproducibly in high CO2 but not in ambient air (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CCMB1:p1A grew reproducibly in an anoxic mix of 10:90 CO2:N2.
source: When expressing rubisco and prk from the p1A plasmid, CCMB1 also grew reproducibly in an anoxic mix of 10:90 CO2:N2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) implying that carboxylation is sufficient for growth on glycerol media and rubisco-catalyzed oxygenation of RuBP is not required.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Carboxylation is sufficient for growth on glycerol media and rubisco-catalyzed oxygenation of RuBP is not required.
source: When expressing rubisco and prk from the p1A plasmid, CCMB1 also grew reproducibly in an anoxic mix of 10:90 CO2:N2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) implying that carboxylation is sufficient for growth on glycerol media and rubisco-catalyzed oxygenation of RuBP is not required.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing growth in anoxic conditions.

claim: pCB encodes 10 carboxysome genes including rubisco large and small subunits, along with prk.
source: pCB encodes 10 carboxysome genes (Bonacci et al., 2012; Cai et al., 2008), including rubisco large and small subunits, along with prk.
evidence: This is a description of the plasmid construction supported by citations.

claim: pCCM encodes putative rubisco chaperones and an inorganic carbon transporter.
source: The remaining H. neapolitanus genes, including putative rubisco chaperones (Aigner et al., 2017; Mueller-Cajar, 2017; Wheatley et al., 2014) and an inorganic carbon transporter (Desmarais et al., 2019; Scott et al., 2019), were cloned into the second plasmid, pCCM.
evidence: This is a description of the plasmid construction supported by citations.

claim: CCMB1 co-transformed with pCB and pCCM initially failed to grow on glycerol media.
source: CCMB1 co-transformed with pCB and pCCM initially failed to grow on glycerol media.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results.

claim: Selection experiments resulted in the isolation of mutant plasmids conferring growth in ambient air.
source: We therefore conducted selection experiments, described fully in Appendix 2, that ultimately resulted in the isolation of mutant plasmids conferring growth in ambient air.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results.

claim: Colonies became visible after 20 days of incubation in ambient air, but only when induction and both plasmids were provided.
source: Colonies became visible after 20 days of incubation in ambient air, but only when induction and both plasmids were provided (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deep-sequencing of plasmid DNA revealed mutations in regulatory sequences but none in sequences coding for CCM components.
source: Deep-sequencing of plasmid DNA revealed mutations in regulatory sequences (e.g. a promoter and transcriptional repressor) but none in sequences coding for CCM components (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data.

claim: pCB' and pCCM' together enabled reproducible growth of CCMB1 in ambient air.
source: As shown in Figure 3, pCB' and pCCM' together enabled reproducible growth of CCMB1 in ambient air, suggesting that the 20 genes expressed are sufficient to produce a heterologous CCM without any genomic mutations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The 20 genes expressed are sufficient to produce a heterologous CCM without any genomic mutations.
source: As shown in Figure 3, pCB' and pCCM' together enabled reproducible growth of CCMB1 in ambient air, suggesting that the 20 genes expressed are sufficient to produce a heterologous CCM without any genomic mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing growth with plasmids alone.

claim: An inactivating mutation to the carboxysomal rubisco (CbbL K194M) prohibited growth entirely.
source: An inactivating mutation to the carboxysomal rubisco (CbbL K194M) prohibited growth entirely.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: An inactive mutant of the carboxysomal carbonic anhydrase (CsoSCA C173S) required high-CO2 for growth.
source: Consistent with this understanding, an inactive mutant of the carboxysomal carbonic anhydrase (CsoSCA C173S) required high-CO2 for growth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Disruption of carboxysome formation by removal of the pentameric shell proteins eliminated growth in ambient air.
source: Similarly, disruption of carboxysome formation by removal of the pentameric shell proteins or the N-terminal domain of CsoS2 also eliminated growth in ambient air.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Truncating CsoS2 prohibits carboxysome formation entirely.
source: Removing the pentameric proteins CsoS4AB disrupts the permeability barrier at the carboxysome shell (Cai et al., 2009), while truncating CsoS2 prohibits carboxysome formation entirely (Oltrogge et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oltrogge et al., 2020.

claim: An inactivating mutation to the inorganic carbon transporter eliminated growth in ambient air.
source: Finally, an inactivating mutation to the inorganic carbon transporter also eliminated growth in ambient air (Desmarais et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation.

claim: Regular polyhedral inclusions of approximately 100 nm diameter were visible in micrographs of CCMB1:pCB'+pCCM'.
source: Regular polyhedral inclusions of ≈100 nm diameter were visible in micrographs (Figure 5A), implying production of morphologically normal carboxysomes.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Carboxysomes from CCMB1:pCB'+pCCM' were similar in appearance to those from the native host, although more heterogeneous in size and shape.
source: Carboxysomes from CCMB1:pCB'+pCCM' were similar in appearance to those from the native host, although more heterogeneous in size and shape (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The rubisco complex was visible inside isolated carboxysomes and confirmed to co-migrate with the structure via SDS-PAGE analysis.
source: The rubisco complex was visible inside isolated carboxysomes and confirmed to co-migrate with the structure via SDS-PAGE analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Serine from CCMB1:pCB'+pCCM' cells contained roughly threefold more 12C than the rubisco-independent control.
source: Consistent with this expectation, serine from CCMB1:pCB'+pCCM' cells contained roughly threefold more 12C than the rubisco-independent control (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by isotopic labeling data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Rubisco carboxylation was responsible for at least 10% of 3PG synthesis in all four biological replicates.
source: Based on these estimates, rubisco carboxylation was responsible for at least 10% of 3PG synthesis in all four biological replicates (Figure 6C, Materials and methods), confirming fixation of CO2 from ambient air.
evidence: This is supported by isotopic labeling data and flux analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: This work represents the first functional reconstitution of any CCM.
source: As such, this work represents the first functional reconstitution of any CCM.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work based on the experimental results.

claim: The α-carboxysome CCM from H. neapolitanus can be readily transferred between species.
source: Here, we demonstrated that the ɑ-carboxysome CCM from H. neapolitanus can be readily transferred between species and confers a large growth benefit, suggesting that these CCMs became so widespread by horizontal transfer between bacteria (Kerfeld and Melnicki, 2016; Rae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results of successful reconstitution.

claim: The transplanted CCM confers a large growth benefit.
source: Here, we demonstrated that the ɑ-carboxysome CCM from H. neapolitanus can be readily transferred between species and confers a large growth benefit, suggesting that these CCMs became so widespread by horizontal transfer between bacteria (Kerfeld and Melnicki, 2016; Rae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing growth in ambient air with the CCM.

claim: These CCMs became widespread by horizontal transfer between bacteria.
source: Here, we demonstrated that the ɑ-carboxysome CCM from H. neapolitanus can be readily transferred between species and confers a large growth benefit, suggesting that these CCMs became so widespread by horizontal transfer between bacteria (Kerfeld and Melnicki, 2016; Rae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and supported by citations.

claim: At most 20 gene products are required to produce a bacterial CCM.
source: These results conclusively demonstrate that at most 20 gene products are required to produce a bacterial CCM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing successful reconstitution with 20 genes.

claim: The α-carboxysome CCM is genetically compact and 'portable' between organisms.
source: The ɑ-carboxysome CCM is apparently genetically compact and 'portable' between organisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: Expressing bacterial CCMs in non-native autotrophic hosts may improve CO2 assimilation and growth.
source: It is possible, therefore, that expressing bacterial CCMs in non-native autotrophic hosts will improve CO2 assimilation and growth.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: The rubisco chaperones are strictly dispensable for producing a functional bacterial CCM.
source: These experiments demonstrated that the rubisco chaperones are strictly dispensable for producing a functional bacterial CCM, although removing acRAF produced a substantial growth defect that warrants further investigation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Removing acRAF produced a substantial growth defect.
source: These experiments demonstrated that the rubisco chaperones are strictly dispensable for producing a functional bacterial CCM, although removing acRAF produced a substantial growth defect that warrants further investigation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: All contemporary Cyanobacteria have CCM genes.
source: Although all contemporary Cyanobacteria have CCM genes, these CCMs are found in two convergently evolved varieties (Flamholz and Shih, 2020; Kerfeld and Melnicki, 2016; Rae et al., 2013), suggesting that the ancestor of present-day Cyanobacteria and chloroplasts did not have a CCM (Rae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature.

claim: Cyanobacterial CCMs are found in two convergently evolved varieties.
source: Although all contemporary Cyanobacteria have CCM genes, these CCMs are found in two convergently evolved varieties (Flamholz and Shih, 2020; Kerfeld and Melnicki, 2016; Rae et al., 2013), suggesting that the ancestor of present-day Cyanobacteria and chloroplasts did not have a CCM (Rae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature.

claim: The ancestor of present-day Cyanobacteria and chloroplasts did not have a CCM.
source: Although all contemporary Cyanobacteria have CCM genes, these CCMs are found in two convergently evolved varieties (Flamholz and Shih, 2020; Kerfeld and Melnicki, 2016; Rae et al., 2013), suggesting that the ancestor of present-day Cyanobacteria and chloroplasts did not have a CCM (Rae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to scientific literature.

claim: Land plant CCMs arose only in the last 100 million years.
source: Land plant CCMs, for example, arose only in the last 100 million years (Flamholz and Shih, 2020; Raven et al., 2017; Sage et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature on CCM evolution.

claim: Pyrenoid CCMs are collectively responsible for perhaps 70–80% of oceanic photosynthesis.
source: Pyrenoid CCMs are collectively responsible for perhaps 70–80% of oceanic photosynthesis (Mackinder et al., 2016; Raven et al., 2017), yet many fundamental questions remain regarding the composition and operation of algal CCMs (Wang and Jonikas, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific literature.

claim: Many fundamental questions remain regarding the composition and operation of algal CCMs.
source: Pyrenoid CCMs are collectively responsible for perhaps 70–80% of oceanic photosynthesis (Mackinder et al., 2016; Raven et al., 2017), yet many fundamental questions remain regarding the composition and operation of algal CCMs (Wang and Jonikas, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: CCMB1 has the genotype BW25113 ΔrpiAB Δedd ΔcynT Δcan.
source: CCMB1 has the genotype BW25113 ΔrpiAB Δedd ΔcynT Δcan and was constructed from ΔrpiAB by deleting both native carbonic anhydrases using the same methods, first transducing the KEIO ΔcynT and then Δcan from EDCM636 (Merlin et al., 2003), which was obtained from the Yale Coli Genetic Stock Center.
evidence: This is a description of the strain construction.

claim: Expressing the full complement of CCM genes led to an increase in culture density of approximately 0.6 OD units after 80 hr of cultivation.
source: Expressing the full complement of CCM genes led to an increase in culture density (optical density at 600 nm) of ≈0.6 units after 80 hr of cultivation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Bootstrapping was used to calculate a 99.9% confidence interval of 0.56–0.64 OD units for the effect of expressing the full CCM during growth in ambient air.
source: Bootstrapping was used to calculate a 99.9% confidence interval of 0.56–0.64 OD units for the effect of expressing the full CCM during growth in ambient air.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis performed on the experimental data.

claim: Maximal growth rates for the 'full CCM' cultures ranged from 0.03 to 0.06 hr−1, corresponding to doubling times of 12–25 hr.
source: Maximal growth rates for the 'full CCM' cultures ranged from 0.03 to 0.06 hr−1, corresponding to doubling times of 12–25 hr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.
